system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Literature search is not available in this session: judge novelty and mechanism from the data and your reasoning.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 15 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Patient population of interest: cancers with biomarker ~MUT_TP53 (TP53 wild-type (no damaging TP53 mutation)).

Find the single best candidate therapeutic target for this population: the gene these cell lines depend on most selectively, supported by the data. Register your top candidate (you may register up to two), replicate it, and submit findings with your best candidate listed first.

content.thinking:
I'm checking which genes are selectively essential in TP53 wild-type lines, and MDM2, MDM4, and PPM1D come up as the expected p53-pathway dependencies. MDM2 is flagged as broadly essential, but its selectivity gap is still large, so I'm weighing whether it counts as selective.

I'm confirming that the "altered" lines are the TP53 wild-type ones, which makes MDM2 the expected answer. The mechanism is that TP53-WT cells depend on MDM2 to keep p53 suppressed, so knocking it out triggers arrest. I'll register it as a well-established hypothesis, replicate it, and check the association to make sure it isn't driven by lineage.

name: scan_target

content.thinking: MDM2 looks like the textbook p53-wild-type dependency, and its selectivity holds up, with 196 of 241 lines dependent versus 124 of 385 for the rest. Since the finding is well established, I'll register it and replicate it, and only the MDM2 hypothesis is needed for the top candidate.

input.mechanism: TP53 wild-type cells depend on MDM2 E3 ligase to continuously ubiquitinate and degrade p53. Knockout of MDM2 stabilizes functional p53, which induces CDKN1A/p21 and apoptosis, so TP53-WT lines are selectively killed while TP53-mutant lines are not.

name: register_hypothesis

input.mechanism: TP53 wild-type cells depend on MDM2 E3 ligase to continuously ubiquitinate and degrade p53. Knockout of MDM2 stabilizes functional p53, which induces CDKN1A/p21 and apoptosis, so TP53-WT lines are selectively killed while TP53-mutant lines are not.

output: Registered H1_MDM2_TP53WT: ~MUT_TP53 -> more dependent on MDM2. Discovery evidence frozen: t=-19.58, n_altered=241. Replication budget left: 5. Replication passes only if one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad lines and Sanger screens.

findings.claim: In TP53 wild-type cancer cell lines, MDM2 knockout is selectively lethal (discovery beta -0.84, t -19.6; held-out Broad beta -0.79, p=6e-41; independent Sanger beta -0.44, p=8e-17), consistent with MDM2 restraining wild-type p53. Selectivity is strong (mean effect -1.37 in TP53-WT vs -0.45 in others), though MDM2 is also a common dependency in many lines, so the therapeutic window depends on TP53-WT status, which is the intended population.

input.summary: Best candidate for TP53 wild-type cancers is MDM2, the p53 E3 ligase. Its dependency is the strongest selective signal (lineage-adjusted t=-19.6 across 626 lines), and it replicated in held-out Broad lines and in independent Sanger screens. This is a well-established mechanism (MDM2 inhibitors such as nutlins are in clinical use for TP53-WT tumors), so it validates the pipeline rather than offering a novel target. Secondary TP53-WT dependencies in the scan were PPM1D, MDM4, and USP7, all in the same p53-regulatory axis; I did not register or test them. Caveat: MDM2 is also broadly essential in a subset of lines, and the effect is weaker in Sanger.
